prompt: The `/ssr` test failed with a one-second sleep and passed with two. What does the passing version still depend on?

choices.text: Nothing: two seconds comfortably covers the script's second and a half
choices.why: Two seconds covers the delay measured on that machine. A busier server that delivers the script later fails it again.

choices.text: The script arriving within two seconds on every machine it runs on
choices.why: Right. The number is still a guess about speed, only a more generous one.

choices.text: The worker count
choices.why: One worker kept the shared basket out of the timings; it has nothing to do with when the script arrives.

choices.text: The basket being empty first
choices.why: The reset makes the count start at 0, which every version needs; the sleep is the part that guesses.

prompt: With the sleeps, the four tests took 1.3 s, 1.8 s, 2.7 s and 1.1 s. With conditions, they took 0.2 s, 0.27 s, 2.1 s and 0.14 s. How many seconds did the conditions save across the four tests?
Why did the `/ssr` test stay slow after its sleeps were replaced, when the other three became fast?

choices.text: Its assertion has a longer default timeout
choices.why: All four use the same five-second default; none of them reached it.

choices.text: The page itself takes a second and a half to work
choices.why: Right. A condition waits as long as the page needs, and this page needs that long.

choices.text: Waiting for an attribute is slower to check than waiting for a text
choices.why: Each check takes milliseconds; the time is spent waiting for the script, not checking.

choices.text: A leftover sleep in the test
choices.why: The final version has no sleep at all; its 2.1 s is the page's own delay.

prompt: With an implicit wait of five seconds, a test finds the banana button on `/ssr` and clicks it 144 ms after the page loaded. What happens?

choices.text: The click waits until the button works
choices.why: The implicit wait applies to finding elements, not to clicking one already found.

choices.text: Nothing: the click is lost and the basket stays at 0
choices.why: Right. The button existed, so the wait ended at once, and its handler had not arrived.

choices.text: `findElement` waits the full five seconds first
choices.why: It returns as soon as something matches; the run found the button in 30 ms.

choices.text: Selenium throws, because the button is not ready
choices.why: Nothing in the button says it is not ready; it is enabled and visible, and the click is delivered to a page that ignores it.

prompt: A team wants an implicit wait to cover "the error message disappears after a fix". Why can it not?

choices.text: It is limited to five seconds
choices.why: Its length is whatever the session sets; the limit is in what it waits for, not how long.

choices.text: It only works with CSS, and the message needs XPath
choices.why: The implicit wait applies to any locator, XPath included, as the count in the script showed.

choices.text: It waits for something to match, never for a match to go away
choices.why: Right. It retries until a locator finds something; an absence ends nothing and costs the whole timeout.

choices.text: Messages are drawn by scripts, and it ignores what scripts add
choices.why: It found the cards in lesson 8, which a script draws; it searches the page as it is at each try.

prompt: A session has an implicit wait of 5000 ms. `driver.wait(until.elementLocated(...), 1000)` waits for an element that never appears. Roughly how many milliseconds pass before it gives up, by the run in this section?
hint: The explicit wait checks its clock only after each call to its condition returns.

prompt: What does `driver.wait(until.elementLocated(By.css('.done')))`, with no second argument, do if `.done` never appears?

choices.text: Fails after five seconds
choices.why: Five seconds is Playwright's assertion default; in `selenium-webdriver` the default timeout is 0.

choices.text: Fails at once, since the timeout is zero
choices.why: Zero does not mean no wait here; the source treats it as no limit.

choices.text: Uses the implicit wait as its timeout
choices.why: The two settings are separate; with the implicit wait at its default, nothing would end the loop.

choices.text: Asks every 200 ms, for ever
choices.why: Right. A timeout of 0, the default, means no limit, so always pass one.

prompt: Match each wait to what it checks.

pairs.right: an element already found has a given text
the element is absent or not visible
the number of matches is exactly eight

prompt: A Playwright test waits for a hidden `<span class="ready">` with `await page.locator('.ready').waitFor()`. The span is added, hidden by CSS. What happens?

choices.text: It returns as soon as the span is in the page
choices.why: That is the `attached` state; with no state given, `waitFor` waits for `visible`.

choices.text: It times out: by default it waits for `visible`
choices.why: Right. A marker hidden with CSS never becomes visible; `{ state: 'attached' }` is the fix.

choices.text: It throws at once, because hidden elements cannot be located
choices.why: Hidden elements can be found; `waitFor` keeps checking their state until the timeout.

choices.text: It checks the span's text instead
choices.why: `waitFor` never looks at text; it waits for one of four states.

prompt: Why does `settled` require the count line to be non-empty as well as `aria-busy` to be `"false"`?

choices.text: `aria-busy` is already `"false"` before the first key
choices.why: Right. On its own it can be true too early; the count line is empty until an answer is drawn.

choices.text: `aria-busy` is not readable from inside the page
choices.why: The function reads it with `getAttribute`, inside the page, like any attribute.

choices.text: To make the typed test pass despite the defect
choices.why: It still fails, on the three fruit; the condition makes it fail fast and honestly.

choices.text: `waitForFunction` needs two conditions at least
choices.why: It takes any function that returns a value; one condition would do if one were enough.

prompt: Match each thing to wait for with the Playwright form that fits it.

pairs.left: a value in `window` that the page sets
a row the server writes to its database
two texts on the page that must agree

prompt: A test wraps `await button.click(); expect(await count.textContent()).toBe('1');` in `expect(async () => {...}).toPass()` on `/ssr`. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: `toPass` cannot contain `await`
choices.why: The block is an async function; awaiting inside it is the normal case.

choices.text: Nothing, since it retries until the click works
choices.why: It does retry, and every retry clicks again; a slow answer can add a second banana.

choices.text: Each retry clicks again, and a later click passes it
choices.why: Right. Keep actions outside `toPass`; the block should only read. It would also hide that the first clicks were ignored.

choices.text: `toPass` waits five seconds before its first try
choices.why: It tries at once and then at growing intervals; five seconds is not part of it.

prompt: A test sets `test.setTimeout(1000)` and then waits with an assertion whose own timeout is 5000 ms. The condition never holds. What does the failure open with?

choices.text: `Timeout: 5000ms`, from the assertion
choices.why: The assertion's clock is never reached; the outer one runs out four seconds earlier.

choices.text: `Test timeout of 1000ms exceeded`
choices.why: Right. The test's clock ran out first; the call log still names the assertion's 5000 ms.

choices.text: `page.goto: Timeout 1000ms exceeded`
choices.why: The navigation finished; the time ran out during the assertion.

choices.text: It passes once the page is ready, after 1.5 s
choices.why: No step outlives the test's clock; at one second the test is over.

prompt: In the installed Playwright, `actionTimeout` defaults to ___ , which means a click has no limit of its own.
A test that checks the product list starts failing after a release, with `Received: 0` after 5000 ms. A colleague raises its timeout to 10 s and it passes, taking 7 s. What did the change do?

choices.text: Fixed a flaky test that only failed on busy machines
choices.why: It failed every time, at the same line, because the page got slower; that is a change in the shop, not noise.

choices.text: Nothing: the timeout only matters when a test fails
choices.why: It decides which answers count as correct; at 10 s, a six-second empty page now passes.

choices.text: It made the suite accept a page that is six seconds slower
choices.why: Right. The failure was the only report of the slowdown; whether six seconds is acceptable is a performance question.

choices.text: It moved the wait out of the assertion and onto the test's own clock
choices.why: The wait is still the assertion's; only its length changed.

prompt: The toast test failed after 12.4 s with `Received: ""`. What would raising its assertion's timeout to 60 s change?

choices.text: It would pass on a slow machine
choices.why: The toast empties two seconds after the click on any machine; looking longer looks at the empty paragraph longer.

choices.text: Only how long the test takes to fail
choices.why: Right. The text has gone before the assertion starts, and no wait brings it back.

choices.text: It would see the text on its first look
choices.why: The first look comes after the two-second sleep, when the text is already gone.

choices.text: The test would be cut by the test timeout instead
choices.why: True of 60 s against the 30-second default, and it would still fail; the cause stays the order.

prompt: Put the steps of the fixed toast test in order.
items: Click Add to basket on the banana
Expect the toast to say Added Banana
Expect the basket count to be 1
Expect the toast to be empty again
trap: Checking the count before the toast is safe for the count and costs the toast its window.

prompt: A page shows *Saving…* for about 300 ms after a click, then *Saved*. Which test is the sound one?

choices.text: Wait 300 ms, then expect *Saving…* to be gone
choices.why: The sleep guesses the duration and checks nothing the user needs.

choices.text: Expect *Saved*, with no sleep before it
choices.why: Right. *Saved* lasts, so a web-first assertion can wait for it as long as saving takes.

choices.text: Expect *Saving…* with a 10 s timeout, then *Saved*
choices.why: A longer timeout cannot catch a 300 ms label that has already gone; it only fails later.

choices.text: Set an implicit wait so *Saved* is found when it appears
choices.why: The element holding the text exists throughout; an implicit wait would find it at once and read *Saving…*.

prompt: A Selenium suite sets an implicit wait of 10 s and uses `driver.wait(..., 15000)` everywhere. A wait that should fail after 15 s sometimes takes about 20. Following Selenium's documentation, what is the fix?

choices.text: Lower the explicit waits to 5 s so the sum is 15
choices.why: The two do not add up in a fixed way; the result depends on how often the condition calls `findElements`.

choices.text: Raise the implicit wait to 15 s to match
choices.why: That makes each call to the condition block longer, and the overrun worse.

choices.text: Leave the implicit wait at 0 and keep the explicit waits
choices.why: Right. The documentation says not to mix them; with the implicit wait at 0, each wait ends near its own timeout.

choices.text: Lower the polling interval to 50 ms
choices.why: The overrun is inside one blocked call, not between calls; polling faster does not shorten it.

prompt: In `selenium-webdriver`, `driver.wait` asks its condition again every ___ milliseconds unless a fourth argument says otherwise.
A suite's `playwright.config.js` sets `actionTimeout: 10000` under `use`. A click on a button that never appears now fails after how long, and why is that better?

choices.text: After 30 s, as before; the test timeout decides
choices.why: The action now has a clock of its own, shorter than the test's, so it runs out first.

choices.text: After 10 s, and the failure names the click
choices.why: Right. It fails sooner and says `locator.click: Timeout 10000ms exceeded` instead of using up the test.

choices.text: After 5 s, because assertions and actions share a clock
choices.why: They do not: five seconds belongs to assertions, and actions had no limit of their own.

choices.text: At once, since the button is missing
choices.why: Missing now might mean present later; Playwright keeps looking until a clock runs out.
